Beyond its dangers as an individuated practice, white racial contempt reflects wider patterns of social formation and habits of epistemic deference. To explore these dynamics, the power of active and culpable ignorance is examined through an analysis of epistemologies of resistance. Focusing on resistant forms of racial ignorance permits (1) a robust sense of the interplay between self and social knowledge, (2) a fluid conception of testimonial and hermeneutical injustice, and (3) a dynamic and interactive account of epistemic responsibility. The constructive sections of the chapter explore how racial contempt often emerges in (1) the narration of space, (2) the experience of racial soundscapes, (3) the disavowal of opacity in the interior and social lives of black people, and (4) the politics of self-trust and social suspicion. This chapter shows how viewing racial contempt as an outgrowth of misplaced deference can enrich repertoires of resistance, conceptually and practically. The philosophical importance of black literary traditions is stated.\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.1093/9780197850084.003.0004\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026, 9, 23]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.31235/osf.io/vsy5m_v1\", \"title\": [\"Political Influencers as Information Sources: Experimental Evidence on Credibility, Belief, and Epistemic Judgment\"], \"abstract\": \"

Political influencers are increasingly important sources of political information on social media, yet how citizens evaluate information attributed to them remains understudied. Using a survey experiment in Canada, we compare how citizens evaluate identical political statements when attributed to influencers, national news, or no source. We examine perceived credibility, belief, and judgment accuracy. Results show that influencer attribution lowers perceived credibility and reduces confidence in accurate political information compared with national news, although these differences vary by ideological orientation. Followers initially report greater belief in false political claims attributed to influencers than recognizers, but this difference weakens substantially after accounting for observed differences between the groups. These findings suggest that influencers’ impact as political information sources depends on both audience characteristics and selection into influencer audiences, underscoring the distinction between audience reach and epistemic authority in hybrid media systems.

\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.31235/osf.io/vsy5m_v1\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026, 10, 16]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.1093/9780197850084.003.0006\", \"title\": [\"The Ethics and Politics of Epistemic Deference\"], \"abstract\": \"Abstract\\n This chapter responds to standard objections against epistemic deference. The first has to do with tensions between political efforts to secure power and the difficulties of making room for complex truths and difficult ambiguities. This chapter recommends deferring to a plurality of epistemic authorities, in addition to the importance of tracking the interests and commitments of cherished exemplars. Second, through a treatment of black collective rituals of autonomy and freedom (like the black national anthem), this chapter answers critics who worry that focusing on deference might discourage openness, creativity, and self-regard. Third, this chapter responds to prominent criticisms of deference epistemologies and their political limitations. It concedes that deference is often co-opted in political practice, but cautions against dismissing the political necessity of representation, structures of earned leadership and authority, and practices of aptly marshaled deference.\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.1093/9780197850084.003.0006\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026, 9, 23]]}}]", "excerpt_truncated": false, "source_sha256": "091850990538319a4105d4d816238a31cccaab8f726916789811656fa56c191c", "verification_required": true, "topic_domain": "judgment_and_consensus", "evidence_role": "discovery", "host_tier": "discovery", "source_identity": null, "persistent_identifiers": ["doi:10.25162/arsp-2022-0013", "doi:10.1093/9780197850084.003.0004", "doi:10.31235/osf.io/vsy5m_v1", "doi:10.1093/9780197850084.003.0006"], "source_candidates": ["https://doi.org/10.25162/arsp-2022-0013", "https://doi.org/10.1093/9780197850084.003.0004", "https://doi.org/10.31235/osf.io/vsy5m_v1", "https://doi.org/10.1093/9780197850084.003.0006"], "source_candidate_identities": {}}
